questions.stem: What is the main purpose of rewards in human resource management?
options: to replace the need for training and performance management
to attract, retain and motivate employees so business goals are met
to meet the legal requirement that every employee receives a bonus
to reduce the total number of employees the business needs to hire
questions.explanation: Rewards are what employees receive in return for their work, and a well-designed reward package helps a business attract, keep and motivate the staff it needs. Bonuses are not a legal requirement.

questions.stem: Base pay is best described as:
options: the fixed wage or salary paid for doing the job
a bonus paid when an individual meets a target
a non-cash extra such as a car or health cover
a share of the business's profit paid each year
questions.explanation: Base pay is the regular wage or salary attached to the role, which must be at least the relevant award or agreement rate. Bonuses and profit shares are performance pay, and cars or health cover are benefits.

questions.stem: A Parramatta real estate agency pays its property managers an annual bonus if their portfolio grows by more than 10%. This is an example of:
options: a common law benefit
performance pay
base pay
job design
questions.explanation: Performance pay links part of an employee's pay to results, such as bonuses, commissions or profit sharing. Base pay is fixed regardless of results.

questions.stem: A Sydney IT firm provides its staff with private health insurance and extra superannuation contributions above the legal minimum. These are examples of:
options: job design, a non-monetary reward
corporate culture, a non-monetary reward
benefits, a type of monetary reward
base pay, a type of monetary reward
questions.explanation: Benefits are extras with a financial value, such as health cover, cars, phones or extra super, provided on top of pay. Non-monetary rewards such as job design and culture have no direct dollar value.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of performance pay?
options: it can only be paid to managers, not to other employees in the business
it is the same for every employee, whatever their level of performance
it can encourage short-term results or competition that harms teamwork
it gives employees no reason at all to work harder or improve results
questions.explanation: Linking pay to targets can motivate, but staff may chase the measured result at the expense of quality, cooperation or long-term goals, and some jobs are hard to measure fairly. Paying everyone the same is a feature of base pay.

questions.stem: Which is a non-monetary reward?
options: giving an employee a company car that can also be used privately on weekends
increasing an employee's annual salary in line with the award
redesigning a job to give an employee more variety and responsibility
paying an employee a Christmas bonus for meeting the year's targets
questions.explanation: Job design, such as adding variety, autonomy or responsibility, rewards employees through more satisfying work rather than money. Bonuses, cars and salary increases all have a monetary value.

questions.stem: A Newcastle accounting firm lets staff work from home two days a week. Which is the most likely limitation of this reward?
options: it raises labour costs because every remote worker must legally be paid more
it is unlawful for employees who are covered by a modern award
it can make supervision, collaboration and team culture harder to maintain
it always lowers employee satisfaction, since staff prefer the office
questions.explanation: Flexible and remote work is valued by many employees and can aid retention, but managers must work harder to coordinate teams, share knowledge and build culture. It does not require higher pay and is not unlawful under awards.

questions.stem: A business pays for an employee to complete a postgraduate qualification. Which is a limitation of development as a reward?
options: the business can no longer claim the cost as an expense
the employee loses their entitlement to annual leave
the employee may leave for another employer once qualified
the employee's skills are likely to decline after the course
questions.explanation: Development rewards staff with new skills and career prospects and builds human capital, but the investment may benefit a competitor if the employee leaves. Some firms ask staff to repay costs if they leave soon after.

questions.stem: Exit interviews at a Wollongong engineering firm show that skilled staff are leaving because of long hours and a lack of recognition, not low pay. Which reward change best targets the problem?
options: introduce flexible hours and a culture of regular recognition
raise base pay by 5% for every employee across the whole business
introduce a commission on each project completed on time
cut benefits so that the savings can fund extra overtime
questions.explanation: The reward should match what employees value: here, work-life balance and recognition, which flexible work and a supportive culture provide. A general pay rise addresses a cause the interviews ruled out, and more incentive to work longer may worsen the problem.

questions.stem: Which is a type of voluntary separation?
options: retrenchment
misconduct-based dismissal
performance-based dismissal
resignation
questions.explanation: Voluntary separation is initiated by the employee: resignation, retirement or accepting voluntary redundancy. Retrenchment and dismissal are involuntary because the employer ends the employment.

questions.stem: A Sydney council invites staff in a department being downsized to apply to leave in return for a redundancy package. Staff who accept are taking:
options: misconduct-based dismissal
voluntary redundancy
retrenchment
retirement
questions.explanation: In voluntary redundancy the employer needs fewer staff but lets employees choose to leave with a package. Retrenchment is involuntary: the employer selects whose job ends.

questions.stem: A factory closes one production line because of falling demand and ends the employment of the 15 workers on it. This is:
options: retrenchment
performance-based dismissal
voluntary redundancy
resignation
questions.explanation: Retrenchment is involuntary separation because the job is no longer needed, not because of anything the employee did. Performance-based dismissal relates to the employee's work.

questions.stem: A warehouse employee deliberately disables a safety guard on a forklift, putting colleagues at risk. If the employer ends her employment, this is most likely:
options: voluntary redundancy
misconduct-based dismissal
performance-based dismissal
retrenchment
questions.explanation: Misconduct-based dismissal follows wrongful behaviour such as serious safety breaches, theft or violence; for serious misconduct, notice does not have to be given. Performance-based dismissal follows a failure to meet job standards after warnings and support.

questions.stem: Before a performance-based dismissal, a fair employer would normally:
options: transfer the employee's role to a contractor without telling them
explain the problem, give warnings, offer support and allow time to improve
dismiss the employee immediately without notice to avoid any dispute
offer the employee a voluntary redundancy package instead of warnings
questions.explanation: Procedural fairness means the employee knows the standard expected, is warned, is supported and has a genuine chance to improve, with the process documented. Skipping these steps exposes the employer to an unfair dismissal claim.

questions.stem: A retailer retrenches 40 staff to cut labour costs. Which is the best assessment of the costs and benefits of this separation?
options: labour costs fall, but redundancy pay, lost skills and lower morale are costs
labour costs fall, and there are no further costs once the staff have left
labour costs rise, because remaining staff must be paid the departing staff's wages
there are no benefits, because separation always reduces a business's profit
questions.explanation: Separation can lower ongoing labour costs and reshape the workforce, but brings costs such as redundancy pay, lost knowledge, recruitment later if demand returns, and anxiety among remaining staff. Both sides must be weighed.

questions.stem: A business asks for volunteers rather than choosing which staff to retrench. Which is the most likely trade-off?
options: more conflict and lower morale, but it can choose exactly which staff to keep
no redundancy pay is owed, but the process takes far longer to complete
no change in morale, but every volunteer must be offered a new position
less conflict and better morale, but its best staff may be the ones who leave
questions.explanation: Voluntary redundancy lets employees choose, which usually reduces conflict and damage to morale. The risk is that highly skilled staff, who can easily find new jobs, are the most likely to volunteer.

questions.stem: Which shows the role of performance management in all three of development, rewards and dismissal?
options: appraisals set the award wage, the NES and the length of the notice period
appraisals identify training needs, set bonus levels and document underperformance
appraisals replace training, remove bonuses and allow dismissal without warning
appraisals are used only once an employee has already been dismissed for misconduct
questions.explanation: Performance management sets goals and gives feedback, so it reveals development needs, provides evidence for performance pay and promotion, and records underperformance and warnings that support a fair dismissal. Awards and the NES are set by law, not appraisals.

questions.stem: Compared with a permanent employee, a casual employee usually:
options: is guaranteed a set number of hours each week for an indefinite period
is not covered by any minimum pay rates under awards or agreements
receives a casual loading instead of paid annual and personal leave
receives paid annual leave and a higher rate of pay for the same work
questions.explanation: Casuals are paid a loading on top of the base rate to compensate for not receiving entitlements such as paid annual and personal leave or notice of termination. They are still covered by award or agreement pay rates.

questions.stem: Under the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), which best describes when an employee is a casual?
options: there is no firm advance commitment to ongoing work, and casual loading or a casual rate applies
the employee works fewer than 38 hours a week for the same employer on a regular basis
the employee has worked for the business for less than 12 months, whatever the hours
the employee is under 21, studying full time, and paid a junior rate of pay
questions.explanation: From 26 August 2024, an employee is casual only if there is no firm advance commitment to continuing and indefinite work, and they are entitled to a casual loading or casual pay rate. Part-time employees also work fewer than 38 hours but are permanent.

questions.stem: The National Employment Standards (NES) are:
options: voluntary guidelines that employers may choose to adopt or simply ignore
rules for employers in NSW only, made by the NSW Parliament
minimum entitlements that awards, agreements and contracts cannot go below
the pay rates for each occupation, set separately for each industry
questions.explanation: The NES are minimum entitlements in the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for national system employees, such as annual leave, personal leave, maximum weekly hours and notice. An award, enterprise agreement or contract cannot provide less. Industry pay rates are set in modern awards.

questions.stem: Which is an entitlement under the National Employment Standards for a full-time employee?
options: 6 weeks of paid annual leave each year of service
a maximum of 48 ordinary hours of work each week
10 days of paid personal/carer's leave each year
20 days of paid personal/carer's leave each year
questions.explanation: The NES give a full-time employee 10 days of paid personal/carer's leave a year, 4 weeks of paid annual leave (5 for some shiftworkers) and a maximum of 38 hours a week plus reasonable additional hours.

questions.stem: A modern award is:
options: a legal document setting minimum pay and conditions for an industry or occupation
an agreement negotiated between one employer and its own employees
an individual contract signed by an employer and a single employee
a prize given by the government each year to the best employer in each industry
questions.explanation: Modern awards are made by the Fair Work Commission and set minimum wages and conditions, such as penalty rates and allowances, on top of the NES. An agreement between one employer and its employees is an enterprise agreement.

questions.stem: Enterprise bargaining is the process in which:
options: employers in an industry agree among themselves to keep wages below the award
an employer and its employees, often through unions, negotiate an enterprise agreement
the Fair Work Commission sets the same minimum wage for every employee in Australia
an individual employee negotiates a private salary with a recruitment agency
questions.explanation: Enterprise bargaining involves the employer and employees, usually through bargaining representatives such as unions, negotiating pay and conditions. The resulting enterprise agreement must be approved by the Fair Work Commission.

questions.stem: A proposed enterprise agreement removes Sunday penalty rates but raises base pay well above the award. How does the Fair Work Commission apply the better off overall test?
options: it checks that each covered employee would be better off overall than under the award
it rejects the agreement automatically because one award entitlement has been reduced
it approves the agreement if a majority of employees would be better off overall
it compares the agreement only with the employees' current pay, not the award
questions.explanation: The better off overall test is a global comparison with the relevant modern award, so a reduced entitlement can be offset by other benefits. It must be met for each award-covered employee, not just a majority, and the baseline is the award, not current practice.

questions.stem: A common law contract of employment is:
options: an agreement between a union and the government about public sector pay
an individual agreement between an employer and an employee, enforceable in court
a document made by the Fair Work Commission for every worker in an industry
an agreement that allows pay below the award if the employee signs it freely
questions.explanation: A common law contract sets out the terms agreed between one employer and one employee, such as pay, duties and notice. It can add to but cannot reduce the NES or any applicable award or agreement.

questions.stem: A senior manager at a Sydney bank is not covered by an award or enterprise agreement. Which statement about her employment conditions is correct?
options: her employer may set any conditions it likes, since no award or agreement applies
her conditions are set by the award for bank tellers, the closest occupation
she must negotiate an enterprise agreement on her own with the employer
her common law contract sets her conditions, but the NES still apply as a minimum
questions.explanation: Many high-paid managers are award-free and employed under individual common law contracts, but the NES apply to all national system employees. Enterprise agreements cover groups of employees, not one person.

questions.stem: Protected industrial action is:
options: lawful action, such as a strike, taken while bargaining for a new enterprise agreement
any strike that a majority of a business's customers have publicly supported
action taken by employees during the life of an approved enterprise agreement
a lockout of employees ordered by a court because of a safety emergency
questions.explanation: Industrial action is protected from legal action only when taken during bargaining for a proposed enterprise agreement and in line with the Fair Work Act's requirements. Action during the nominal term of an agreement is not protected.

questions.stem: Employees bargaining for a new single-enterprise agreement want to take protected industrial action. Which is required?
options: a vote by the business's customers, then at least 1 working day's notice
an order from the NSW Supreme Court, then 3 months' written notice
a protected action ballot in favour, then at least 3 working days' written notice
approval in writing from the employer, then at least 30 days' written notice
questions.explanation: Employee action must be authorised by a protected action ballot ordered by the Fair Work Commission, and the employer must receive at least 3 working days' written notice, or a longer period set by the Commission, after the result is declared. Employer consent is not required.

questions.stem: Anti-discrimination laws such as the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) and the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) make it unlawful to:
options: dismiss an employee for serious misconduct after a fair investigation process
pay a casual employee a loading instead of paid annual and personal leave days
treat a person less favourably at work because of attributes such as sex or age
hire the best qualified applicant for a job ahead of less qualified applicants
questions.explanation: Anti-discrimination laws prohibit treating people less favourably on grounds such as sex, race, age, disability or pregnancy in recruitment, pay, promotion, training and dismissal. Selecting on merit is lawful and is the aim of these laws.

questions.stem: A Dubbo manager passes over a qualified employee for promotion because she is pregnant. This is most likely:
options: lawful, as promotion decisions are not covered by law
unfair dismissal, because her job has ended
unlawful discrimination on the ground of pregnancy
lawful, because the manager is planning ahead
questions.explanation: Pregnancy is a protected attribute under Commonwealth and NSW anti-discrimination law, and promotion decisions are covered. She has not been dismissed, so unfair dismissal does not apply.

questions.stem: Under the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), an unfair dismissal is one that is:
options: made after the employee has worked for the business for 10 years
carried out by a manager rather than by the business's owner
harsh, unjust or unreasonable, and not a case of genuine redundancy
made by a small business employer, whatever the reason or process used
questions.explanation: The Fair Work Commission can find a dismissal unfair if it was harsh, unjust or unreasonable, it was not a genuine redundancy and, for small businesses, it did not follow the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code. Applications must be lodged within 21 days of the dismissal taking effect.

questions.stem: Two employees are dismissed after 8 months' service: Ana at a cafe with 10 employees and Ben at a supermarket with 60 employees. Who has served the minimum employment period to claim unfair dismissal?
options: only Ana
both of them
neither of them
only Ben
questions.explanation: The minimum employment period is 6 months, or 12 months for a small business employer with fewer than 15 employees. Ben's 8 months exceed 6, but Ana's 8 months are short of the 12 she needs.

questions.stem: A Tamworth transport company employed an average of 60 staff during the year. Nine resigned and three were dismissed. What was its voluntary employee turnover?
questions.explanation: Voluntary turnover counts only employees who chose to leave: 9 / 60 x 100 = 15%. Including the three dismissals gives 12 / 60 = 20%, which is total turnover.

questions.stem: A Sydney restaurant has annual revenue of $4.8 million and labour costs of $1.2 million. What is its labour cost percentage?
questions.explanation: Labour cost percentage = labour costs / revenue x 100 = 1.2 / 4.8 x 100 = 25%. Dividing revenue by labour costs gives 4, which is not a percentage of revenue.

questions.stem: A consulting firm with 24 employees earned revenue of $3.6 million. What was its employee productivity measured as revenue per employee?
questions.explanation: Revenue per employee = $3,600,000 / 24 = $150,000. Productivity measures output per employee or per hour worked; a rise means each employee is producing more.

questions.stem: Worker satisfaction is usually measured by:
options: anonymous employee surveys
the business's market share
the number of sales invoices
the business's current ratio
questions.explanation: Employee surveys, often anonymous, ask staff how satisfied and engaged they are with their work, pay, managers and culture. Market share and the current ratio are marketing and finance metrics.

questions.stem: A hotel's voluntary turnover rose from 18% to 30% while the industry benchmark stayed at 20%, and survey scores fell. Which corrective action is most appropriate?
options: recruit more staff from overseas without changing anything else in the hotel
find the causes through exit interviews and surveys, then fix rewards or management
accept the result, because turnover always rises when the economy is growing
cut training spending, since staff are leaving before training pays off
questions.explanation: Turnover now well above both past performance and the benchmark, with falling satisfaction, signals an internal problem. Corrective action should diagnose the cause and address it, for example through rewards, flexibility or leadership. Cutting training would likely worsen satisfaction.

questions.stem: A cafe's revenue stayed at $2 million, but its labour costs rose from $560,000 to $680,000. Which interpretation and response fit best?
options: labour cost percentage rose from 28% to 34%, so it should cut menu prices immediately
labour cost percentage rose from 28% to 34%, so it should review rosters and productivity
labour cost percentage fell from 34% to 28%, so it should hire more staff at once
labour cost percentage is unchanged because revenue did not change during the year
questions.explanation: $560,000 / $2,000,000 = 28% and $680,000 / $2,000,000 = 34%, so labour now uses a larger share of revenue. Corrective action targets labour cost efficiency, such as better rostering or training to lift productivity. Cutting prices would lower revenue and push the percentage higher.

questions.stem: A luxury hotel's strategy is to differentiate on exceptional service. Which HR decision is best aligned with this strategy?
options: freeze recruitment so that remaining staff cover larger areas of the hotel
invest in service training and reward staff for guest satisfaction scores
replace experienced staff with casuals on minimum pay to cut labour costs
remove all performance feedback so that staff feel less pressure at work
questions.explanation: HR decisions should support the business strategy: differentiation on service needs skilled, engaged staff, so development and service-linked rewards fit. Cutting skills and staffing levels may lower costs but undermines the service that justifies premium prices.

questions.stem: Which best shows the interdependence of human resources with the finance function?
options: human resources prepares the balance sheet and income statement each year
the finance budget limits what the business can spend on pay rises and training
human resources sets the prices that marketing charges for the business's products
finance decides which applicants are best suited to each vacant position
questions.explanation: Labour is often a business's largest cost, so reward and development plans must fit the finance budget, while finance depends on a productive workforce to reach profit targets. Pricing and financial reporting are not HR's role.
